05 · Extremes: RX1day, TXx and R95p¶

Question for this notebook. How well do the two EERIE models reproduce heavy-rainfall and hot-day extremes over north-west Europe, and over the UK and Ireland in particular?

Data. Daily precipitation and daily maximum temperature, 1985–2014, on the north-west Europe box (20°W–13°E, 40–65°N, 0.25° grid): ICON-ESM-ER r1, IFS-FESOM2-SR r1, the ERA5 reanalysis reference, and E-OBS, a station-based gridded dataset that covers land only.

Method (fixed in docs/methods.md before any result was produced). Three standard indices, each computed at every grid cell, once per calendar year and once per winter (December–February):

Index Plain meaning
RX1day The wettest single day of the year (or winter), in mm.
TXx The hottest day of the year (or winter): the highest daily maximum temperature, in °C.
R95p How much rain fell on the very wet days of the year (or winter), in mm. A day is "very wet" if it exceeds the local 95th percentile of wet days (see Background).

Annual indices are the general description of extremes. Winter indices exist because the next notebook relates extremes to the winter NAO.

Sections

  1. Setup and data check
  2. Findings
  3. RX1day: the wettest day of the year
  4. R95p: rain on very wet days
  5. TXx: the hottest day of the year
  6. Winter versions of the indices
  7. Regional numbers, land only
  8. Year-to-year behaviour
  9. Saved outputs
  10. Limitations

Background: the terms used in this notebook¶

If you know these already, skip to section 1.

Term What it means here
Extreme index A single number per year that summarises the extreme end of daily weather, defined the same way everywhere so that datasets can be compared. These three come from the ETCCDI list used in IPCC reports.
Wet day A day with at least 1 mm of precipitation. Days with less are treated as dry, because models tend to produce far too many days of drizzle.
95th percentile of wet days The daily amount exceeded on only the wettest 5% of wet days at that place, over 1985–2014. It is a local threshold: about 15 mm in a dry region, 50 mm or more on a wet mountain coast.
R95p The total rain that fell on days above that threshold, added up over the year. The whole day's rain is counted, not just the part above the threshold. Also shown as a share (%) of all wet-day rain.
Base period The years used to define the threshold, here 1985–2014. Using the same years to define and to apply a threshold makes exceedances slightly less frequent than the nominal 5% (Zhang et al. 2005); this small effect is the same for every dataset and is not corrected.
Winter (DJF) December–February, named after the year of its January. Winter 1985 has no December 1984 in the data, so there are 29 complete winters, 1986–2014.
ERA5 Reanalysis reference. Its temperature is well constrained by observations; its precipitation is produced by a weather model.
E-OBS Daily maps built from weather-station measurements, land only. A more direct record of rainfall than ERA5, but station maps smooth out the most intense local rain, so E-OBS extremes tend to be on the low side.
Land-only regional mean The average over the land grid cells of a region. Used for the headline numbers because extremes matter where people live and E-OBS has no data over sea.
Percent difference 100 × (model − reference) ÷ reference. +30% means the model's value is 30% larger.

How to read the maps. Maps of an index use one blue scale, light to dark. Difference maps use blue–grey–orange: grey means no difference; the caption says which direction each colour is. All panels of one figure share one colour scale.

Colours of the lines. Dark grey is ERA5, light grey is E-OBS, blue is ICON-ESM-ER, orange is IFS-FESOM2-SR, as in every notebook of this project.

What a 0.25° grid can and cannot show. A grid cell is roughly 25 km across. Its "daily rainfall" is an average over that area, so it is always lower than what a single rain gauge inside it could record in a thunderstorm. All four datasets are compared on the same 0.25° grid.

1. Setup and data check¶

What this cell does. Loads the project code. The index definitions are in eerie_uk/extremes.py; each has a unit test on a small made-up series with a known answer.

In [1]:
import sys, warnings
sys.path.insert(0, '../src')
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
from pathlib import Path
from eerie_uk import climatology as clim, extremes as ex, plotting, regions, store

MODELS = ['icon-esm-er', 'ifs-fesom2-sr']
REFS = ['e-obs', 'era5']      # reference datasets
SOURCES = REFS + MODELS
NAME = plotting.SOURCE_LABELS

What this cell does. Computes all indices for each source: the local 95th-percentile threshold, then RX1day, R95p, the R95p share and TXx, per year and per winter. The first run reads about 11,000 daily maps per variable and takes about a minute per source; the result is saved under data/derived/ so later runs are instant.

In [3]:
indices = {s: ex.indices_for(s) for s in SOURCES}
pd.DataFrame([{'source': NAME[s], 'years': indices[s].sizes['year_ann'], 'winters': indices[s].sizes['year_djf'],
               'grid (lat x lon)': f"{indices[s].sizes['lat']} x {indices[s].sizes['lon']}",
               'cells with data %': 100 * float(indices[s].rx1day_ann.isel(year_ann=0).notnull().mean())} for s in SOURCES])

What this cell does. Puts E-OBS on the same grid points as the models. E-OBS uses a 0.25° grid shifted by half a cell, so its index maps are interpolated (bilinearly) to the model grid. It also builds a land mask from the Natural Earth coastline, for the land-only averages, and keeps the land cells where E-OBS has data as the common set used for all regional numbers.

In [4]:
grid = indices['icon-esm-er']
indices['e-obs'] = regions.to_grid(indices['e-obs'], grid)
land = regions.land_mask(grid.lat, grid.lon)
observed = indices['e-obs'].rx1day_ann.isel(year_ann=0).notnull() & indices['e-obs'].txx_ann.isel(year_ann=0).notnull()
common = land & observed      # the same cells are used for every dataset in regional averages
print(f'land cells: {int(land.sum())} of {land.size} ({100 * float(land.mean()):.0f}%); land cells with E-OBS data: {int(common.sum())}')

def mean_map(source, name):
    'Average of an index over all its years.'
    field = indices[source][name]
    return field.mean([d for d in field.dims if d.startswith('year')])

def percent_difference(a, b):
    return 100 * (a - b) / b

land cells: 4446 of 13433 (33%); land cells with E-OBS data: 3735

2. Findings¶

Numbers are 1985–2014 averages over UK and Ireland land (the same land cells for every dataset). One member per model. Two references: E-OBS (station-based) and ERA5 (reanalysis).

UK and Ireland, land E-OBS ERA5 ICON-ESM-ER IFS-FESOM2-SR
Wettest day of the year (RX1day) 30.9 mm 28.6 mm 45.7 mm 33.4 mm
… model difference from E-OBS / from ERA5 +48% / +60% +8% / +17%
Rain on very wet days per year (R95p) 181 mm 173 mm 274 mm 196 mm
… model difference from E-OBS / from ERA5 +52% / +59% +9% / +14%
Share of rain that falls on very wet days 17.7% 17.9% 19.8% 19.1%
Hottest day of the year (TXx) 26.9 °C 25.5 °C 23.6 °C 25.0 °C
… model difference from E-OBS / from ERA5 −3.3 / −2.0 °C −1.9 / −0.6 °C
Wettest winter day, difference from E-OBS / ERA5 +33% / +41% +9% / +16%
Rain on very wet winter days, difference from E-OBS / ERA5 +62% / +83% +9% / +23%

What this means, in plain words

  1. The data are complete: 30 years of daily files for both models and both references, 29 complete winters.
  2. The two references agree closely with each other. ERA5's rainfall extremes are a few percent lower than E-OBS's and its hottest days about 1.4 °C cooler. That spread is the uncertainty in "the observed value" that any model comparison has to live with.
  3. IFS-FESOM2-SR's rainfall extremes are close to both references: within about 10% of E-OBS and 15–20% of ERA5 over UK and Ireland, and within a few percent in north-west France.
  4. ICON-ESM-ER's rainfall extremes are far too heavy against either reference: about +50% to +60% for the year and up to +80% in winter, in all three regions. This continues the chain seen earlier: too-strong westerlies (notebook 03), a mean state like a permanent positive NAO (notebook 04), too much winter rain on average, and now too-heavy extremes. The excess also appears in north-west France and in summer-dominated annual maxima, so the circulation bias is probably not the whole story.
  5. The share of rain on very wet days is similar in all four datasets (18–20%): ICON-ESM-ER rains too much on ordinary and extreme days alike.
  6. Hottest days: with ERA5 the picture becomes clearer. Against E-OBS both models looked too cool by 2–3 °C. Against ERA5, which is on a grid like the models', IFS-FESOM2-SR is only 0.6 °C cooler, so most of its apparent deficit was the comparison of grid cells with low-lying stations, not a model fault. ICON-ESM-ER remains about 2 °C too cool against ERA5, so its hot extremes are genuinely too mild.
  7. Year-to-year spread of the regional extremes is of the right order in both models. ICON-ESM-ER's hottest day varies less from year to year (about 1.0 °C against 1.6 °C in both references), in line with its low temperature variability in notebook 03.

Bottom line. IFS-FESOM2-SR's rainfall and heat extremes are credible against both references. ICON-ESM-ER's rainfall extremes are clearly too heavy and its hottest days too mild. These are exploratory results from one member each.

3. RX1day: the wettest day of the year¶

What this cell does. Maps the average annual RX1day for the four sources: at each place, the wettest day of each year, averaged over the 30 years.

In [5]:
plotting.plot_field_panels({NAME[s]: mean_map(s, 'rx1day_ann') for s in SOURCES}, units='mm',
                           title='Annual RX1day, mean of 1985-2014', columns=2);

Figure 1. Average wettest day of the year. The largest values should follow mountains facing the Atlantic and the Mediterranean (western Norway, western Scotland, north-west Iberia, the Alps and the Cévennes). E-OBS is blank over sea.

What this cell does. Shows each model's RX1day as a percent difference from each reference dataset (one row of maps per reference).

In [6]:
panels = {f'{NAME[m]} vs {NAME[r]}': percent_difference(mean_map(m, 'rx1day_ann'), mean_map(r, 'rx1day_ann'))
          for r in REFS for m in MODELS}
plotting.plot_field_panels(panels, units='% difference', title='Annual RX1day: model relative to each reference', columns=2, diverging=True);

Figure 2. RX1day percent difference. Orange: the model's wettest day is wetter than the reference; blue: drier. E-OBS smooths intense rain, so a model that is somewhat wetter than E-OBS is not necessarily wrong.

4. R95p: rain on very wet days¶

What this cell does. Maps the local threshold that defines a "very wet day" in each source: the 95th percentile of wet-day precipitation. This is worth seeing first, because R95p is measured against each dataset's own threshold.

In [7]:
plotting.plot_field_panels({NAME[s]: indices[s].p95_ann for s in SOURCES}, units='mm/day',
                           title='Threshold for a very wet day (95th percentile of wet days), 1985-2014', columns=2);

Figure 3. The very-wet-day threshold. A model with a higher threshold than the references has heavier heavy-rain days.

What this cell does. Maps the average annual R95p (mm of rain per year that falls on very wet days) for the four sources.

In [8]:
plotting.plot_field_panels({NAME[s]: mean_map(s, 'r95p_ann') for s in SOURCES}, units='mm per year',
                           title='Annual R95p, mean of 1985-2014', columns=2);

Figure 4. Rain falling on very wet days, per year. It is large where it rains a lot overall, so it resembles a map of total rainfall; the next figure removes that effect.

What this cell does. Maps R95p as a share of all wet-day rain. This says how concentrated the rain is in heavy days, independent of how wet the place is.

In [9]:
plotting.plot_field_panels({NAME[s]: mean_map(s, 'r95p_share_ann') for s in SOURCES}, units='% of wet-day rain',
                           title='Share of annual rain that falls on very wet days, 1985-2014', columns=2);

Figure 5. Share of rain from very wet days. By construction it sits near 15–25% almost everywhere, so differences between panels are subtle; it is higher where rain comes in a few intense events (around the Mediterranean) and lower in steady maritime climates.

7. Regional numbers, land only¶

UK and Ireland is the headline region. Western Norway and north-west France are supporting regions on the wet and dry sides of the NAO rainfall pattern.

What this cell does. Averages each index over the land cells of each region, for every year. Exactly the same cells are used for every dataset (land cells where E-OBS has data), so coastal cells that are partly sea in one dataset cannot distort the comparison. It then and collects the results in one long table (series) used for the tables and charts below and saved for the next notebook.

In [15]:
INDEX_LABELS = {'rx1day': 'RX1day (mm)', 'r95p': 'R95p (mm)', 'r95p_share': 'R95p share (%)', 'txx': 'TXx (°C)'}
rows = []
for s in SOURCES:
    for tag, period in (('ann', 'annual'), ('djf', 'winter')):
        for key in INDEX_LABELS:
            field = indices[s][f'{key}_{tag}'].where(common).rename({f'year_{tag}': 'year'})
            for r in regions.SUBREGIONS:
                values = clim.regional_mean(field, r)
                rows += [{'source': s, 'region': r, 'period': period, 'index': key, 'year': int(y), 'value': float(v)}
                         for y, v in zip(values.year.values, values.values)]
series = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(len(series), 'regional values')

2832 regional values

What this cell does. The headline table: the 30-year (or 29-winter) average of each index over UK and Ireland land, for all four sources, with each model's difference from both references. Differences are in % for the rainfall indices and in °C for TXx.

In [16]:
def headline(region):
    mean = series[series.region == region].groupby(['period', 'index', 'source']).value.mean().unstack('source')[SOURCES]
    out = mean.rename(columns=NAME)
    for m in MODELS:
        for r in REFS:
            relative = 100 * (mean[m] - mean[r]) / mean[r]
            absolute = mean[m] - mean[r]
            is_temperature = mean.index.get_level_values('index') == 'txx'
            out[f'{NAME[m]} vs {NAME[r]}'] = np.where(is_temperature, absolute, relative)
    out.index = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([(p, INDEX_LABELS[i]) for p, i in out.index], names=['period', 'index'])
    return out
uk = headline('uk_ireland')
uk

8. Year-to-year behaviour¶

A model and the real world do not share the same sequence of years, so the lines below are not expected to rise and fall together. Compare their level and how much they vary.

What this cell does. Plots annual RX1day (land average) for each year, in the three regions.

In [18]:
def series_panels(index, period):
    panels = {}
    for r in regions.SUBREGIONS:
        part = series[(series.region == r) & (series['index'] == index) & (series.period == period)]
        panels[regions.LABELS[r]] = {s: (part[part.source == s].year.values, part[part.source == s].value.values) for s in SOURCES}
    return panels
plotting.plot_line_panels(series_panels('rx1day', 'annual'), ylabel='mm', xlabel='year', title='Annual RX1day, land average, 1985-2014');

Figure 11. Wettest day of each year, averaged over the land of each region.

What this cell does. The same for annual TXx.

In [19]:
plotting.plot_line_panels(series_panels('txx', 'annual'), ylabel='°C', xlabel='year', title='Annual TXx, land average, 1985-2014');

Figure 12. Hottest day of each year, land average. ERA5 and E-OBS describe the same real years and should move together (2003 and 2006 were hot summers in western Europe); that agreement is a check on the two references.

What this cell does. The same for winter R95p, one of the quantities used in the next notebook.

In [20]:
plotting.plot_line_panels(series_panels('r95p', 'winter'), ylabel='mm per winter', xlabel='winter (year of January)', title='Winter R95p, land average, 1986-2014');

Figure 13. Rain on very wet winter days, land average.

What this cell does. Summarises the year-to-year spread: the standard deviation of each regional series for UK and Ireland, per source. A model whose spread is far from both references has extremes that vary too much or too little from year to year.

10. Limitations¶

  • One member per model and 30 years. A 30-year mean of an annual maximum is still noisy, especially for rainfall. Differences of 10% or so in RX1day at a single grid cell mean little.
  • Neither reference is the truth for rainfall extremes. ERA5 rain is a model product at about 31 km. E-OBS is built from stations and smooths intense local rain, more so where stations are sparse. The models are compared with both, and a conclusion is firm only where both agree.
  • Grid-cell values are area averages (about 25 km), lower than point measurements.
  • ERA5 and E-OBS were interpolated to the model grid bilinearly. For precipitation a conservative method would be preferable; bilinear interpolation slightly smooths maxima.
  • Terrain heights differ between datasets, which affects TXx over mountains.
  • In-base percentile effect (see Background): small and common to all datasets.
  • Annual TXx is a summer quantity and is not related to the winter NAO.
  • 29 winters, not 30, because the first winter lacks its December.

11. Open questions¶

  1. How much of ICON-ESM-ER's excess extreme rainfall comes from its circulation bias, and how much from its precipitation physics? Its excess also appears where the circulation bias is small.
  2. Why are ICON-ESM-ER's hottest days about 2 °C too cool even against ERA5, while its average summer temperature is close to ERA5's?
  3. Would conservative regridding of the references change the rainfall comparison noticeably?
